title: Pastry
intro: Doughs, creams, custards and the sugar work behind the dessert menu. Precision matters most here, so ratios and temperatures lead every entry in the chapter.

entries.title: Crème anglaise
entries.summary: Crème anglaise is the French pouring custard: milk, sugar and vanilla cooked gently with egg yolks until it coats a spoon, and never boiled. It is a sauce in its own right and the base of ice cream, Bavarian cream and île flottante.
entries.guest: Crème anglaise is a silky vanilla custard sauce, poured rather than set. On our Pineapple Tarte Tatin it is made with sweetened condensed milk, for a caramelised milk flavour.

paras: Crème anglaise, English cream in French, is a pouring custard: milk, or milk and cream, sweetened, scented with vanilla and thickened by egg yolks alone, with no flour or cornflour. Stirred over gentle heat, the yolk proteins set just enough to turn the milk into a silky sauce. Kitchens call that point nappe, from the French for a cloth: the sauce lies on the back of a spoon like a thin cloth, and a finger drawn through it leaves a clean line that does not run back.
It is the first custard a pastry cook learns and the one many others grow from. Served warm or cold, it sauces tarts, puddings and poached fruit.

A common working ratio is 1 litre (about 1 quart) of milk, or milk and cream, to 8 to 10 yolks and 150 to 200 g (5 to 7 oz) of sugar, with a split vanilla pod. More yolks give a thicker, richer sauce. More cream makes it richer and fuller in body, though the set itself comes from the yolks alone. Recipes vary, so the house recipe is always the one to follow.

Bring the milk to a simmer with half the sugar and the split vanilla pod, then take it off the heat and let the vanilla infuse for ten minutes or so. Whisk the yolks with the rest of the sugar until pale, and do it at once: sugar left sitting on yolks dries them into hard specks. Pour about a third of the hot milk onto the yolks, whisking all the while. This is tempering, warming the yolks gradually so they thicken the milk instead of scrambling in it. Then pour the warmed yolks back into the pan.

Cook over low to medium heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon or a heatproof spatula in a figure of eight, reaching into the corners where the pan runs hottest. The foam on top subsides and the sauce thickens slightly. Take it to 82 to 84°C (180 to 183°F), where it coats the spoon, and never let it boil. Strain it at once through a fine sieve into a cold bowl set over ice, stir now and then as the heat leaves it, then cover and chill.

Flavour an anglaise by infusing the milk with coffee beans, citrus zest, tea or spices, strained out before the yolks go in, or stir melted chocolate or a liqueur into the strained sauce. Churned in an ice cream machine, the same base becomes French vanilla ice cream. Set with gelatine and folded with whipped cream, it becomes a Bavarian cream, which has its own entry. Under spoonfuls of meringue poached in milk it is œufs à la neige, snow eggs, which most kitchens now call île flottante, floating island.

Curdled: the sauce went past about 85°C (185°F), often at the bottom of the pan, and the yolks set into grains. Caught early, pour it straight into a cold bowl, blend it or whisk hard, and strain; truly scrambled, start again. Thin: it came off the heat before nappe, so the yolks never thickened it; return it to gentle heat and keep stirring. A skin: it cooled uncovered and the surface dried; press cling film onto the surface or stir it as it cools.

At Brennan's the anglaise is the sweetened condensed anglaise on the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, the kitchen's twist on the classic. Sweetened condensed milk, which is milk cooked down with sugar until thick, gives the custard a caramel note like dulce de leche, the slow-cooked milk caramel of Latin America. It is poured beside the charred pineapple and puff pastry, cool and silky against the hot caramel. The kitchen also makes its own vanilla ice cream for the flamed desserts; whether it starts from an anglaise is a question for the kitchen.

Say anglaise as ahn-GLEZ. To a guest it is a pouring vanilla custard, lighter than ice cream and silkier than cream; on the tarte Tatin, a pouring custard with a caramelised milk flavour. It is made with egg yolks and milk, so any allergy or dietary question goes to the service note and the kitchen before the order, never to a guess at the table.

entries.title: Crème pâtissière
entries.summary: Crème pâtissière, pastry cream, is milk, sugar and egg yolks thickened with flour or cornflour and boiled until it holds its shape. It fills éclairs, tarts and mille-feuille, and is the parent of diplomate, mousseline, chiboust and frangipane.
entries.guest: Pastry cream is a thick vanilla custard, the filling inside an éclair or under the fruit on a tart: smooth, rich and set enough to pipe.

paras: Crème pâtissière, the pastry cook's cream, is a custard thickened with starch as well as egg yolk: milk, sugar, yolks and flour or cornflour, cooked on the stove until thick enough to pipe, spread or slice. Where crème anglaise pours, pastry cream holds its shape. It is the workhorse filling of the French pastry kitchen: inside éclairs and profiteroles, under the fruit of a fruit tart, between the sheets of a mille-feuille, the layered puff pastry slice, and loosened with yolks and flavour as the base of a soufflé.

The one rule to learn first is the opposite of the anglaise rule. Anglaise must never boil. Pastry cream must boil, for a minute or two, and the starch is what allows it: the swelling starch granules stand between the yolk proteins, so they cannot knot together into curds.

A dependable working ratio is 500 ml (about 2 cups) of milk to 4 to 6 yolks, 100 to 125 g (about 4 oz) of sugar and 40 to 50 g (about 1.5 oz) of starch, with vanilla and, for richness, 25 to 50 g (1 to 2 oz) of butter whisked in at the end. Cornflour gives a cleaner, glossier cream that sets firmer; flour gives a softer one and needs its full boil to lose its raw taste. Many cooks use a mix, and the house recipe decides.

Bring the milk to the boil with about half the sugar and a split vanilla pod. Whisk the yolks with the rest of the sugar, then whisk in the starch until smooth. Pour about a third of the hot milk onto the yolks, whisking, to temper them, then return everything to the pan.

Cook over medium heat, whisking constantly and reaching into the corners. The cream thickens suddenly and may look lumpy; keep whisking and it turns smooth. When big, slow bubbles break the surface, keep whisking for one to two minutes more. That boil does two jobs. It swells the starch fully, so the cream thickens and loses any floury taste. And it destroys amylase, an enzyme in egg yolk that digests starch; left alive, it turns a thick cream to soup in the fridge overnight. Off the heat, whisk in the butter.

Spread the cream thinly in a lined tray, press cling film directly onto the surface so no skin forms, and chill it quickly. Cold, it sets stiff and rubbery. Before use, beat it briefly with a whisk or paddle until smooth again, and stop there: long, hard beating breaks the starch and thins it.

Four classic creams grow from it. Crème diplomate folds in whipped cream, often with a little gelatine, for a lighter filling in tarts and choux. Crème mousseline beats in soft butter for a rich, silky cream that holds up in layered cakes; flavoured with praline, it fills the Paris-Brest. Crème chiboust folds in Italian meringue, usually with gelatine, and fills a classic Paris cake crowned with caramel-glazed choux puffs; by the usual account it is named for Chiboust, a Paris pastry cook of the 1840s. Frangipane mixes pastry cream with almond cream, crème d'amande, and bakes inside tarts and the galette des rois, the puff pastry king cake of Epiphany. Italian meringue and choux have their own entries.

Runny the next day: it did not boil long enough, and the yolk's amylase thinned it; it cannot be mended, so give it the full boil next time. Lumpy: the heat was too high or the whisk stopped; whisk hard off the heat, or pass it through a sieve while hot. Scorched: the whisk missed the corners; pour the cream into a clean bowl without scraping the bottom, and taste it, because a burnt taste means starting again. A tough skin: no cling film on the surface.

Pastry cream rarely appears by name on a menu; it is the cream inside. Describe it as a thick vanilla custard, the éclair filling. A guest who knows Boston cream pie knows it already: it is the cream between the sponge layers. It is made with milk, eggs and flour or cornflour, so any allergy question goes to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Sabayon
entries.summary: Sabayon is egg yolks, sugar and wine whisked over simmering water into a warm, airy foam. Sweet, it sauces fruit; savoury, made with Champagne or stock, it glazes fish and oysters. The same foam is the first stage of a hollandaise.
entries.guest: Sabayon is a warm, airy sauce of egg yolks whisked with wine until they froth, light as a cloud, with a gentle note of the wine.

paras: Sabayon is a foam, not a set custard. Egg yolks, sugar and wine are whisked together in a bowl over barely simmering water until the yolks swell with air and thicken just enough to hold it. The result is warm, pale and light, often three times the volume it started at, and it is served soon, because a sabayon slowly sinks as it stands. The Italian original is zabaglione, or zabaione, made with Marsala, the fortified wine of Sicily; the French name comes from the Italian.

It is a lesson in control: the cook takes yolks to the edge of setting and stops there, by eye. The same foam, yolks whisked over heat to a ribbon, is the first stage of a hollandaise, so a cook who can make a sabayon already knows the first half of a hollandaise.

Allow about one yolk a person, with about 25 g (2 tbsp) of sugar and 30 to 50 ml (2 to 3 tbsp) of wine for each yolk. Less sugar gives a drier foam that tastes more of the wine; more wine gives a lighter foam that holds less well. For a savoury sabayon the sugar goes, and Champagne, a white wine reduction or a little stock takes the place of the sweet wine, with a pinch of salt.

Use a round-bottomed bowl, copper or stainless steel, that sits over a pan of barely simmering water, around 90°C (194°F), without touching it. Whisk the yolks and sugar until pale, add the wine, set the bowl over the water and whisk without stopping, right round the sides and across the bottom, where the egg cooks fastest. Lift the bowl off for a moment if it grows too hot to hold a hand against.

First the mixture froths, loose and bubbly. Then it swells, turns pale and thickens. The cue is the ribbon: lift the whisk and the foam falls back in a thick band that sits on the surface for a few seconds before sinking, and the whisk leaves a trail across the bottom of the bowl. For a batch for four this usually takes five to ten minutes. A probe in the foam reads about 71 to 75°C (160 to 167°F) at the ribbon; the sugar and wine let a sweet sabayon take a little more heat than the plain yolks of a hollandaise. Stop there; a little longer and the yolks scramble at the edges.
Serve it warm at once, or whisk it over ice until cold and fold in whipped cream to hold it longer.

Savoury sabayon is made without sugar, with Champagne, a white wine reduction or a little fish stock, and seasoned with salt and lemon. It is spooned over poached fish or warm oysters on the half shell and glazed under the salamander, the fierce overhead grill of a restaurant kitchen, until it browns in patches. In the classical kitchen a spoonful of sabayon or hollandaise is folded into a white wine fish sauce so it glazes evenly under the salamander.

Sweet, a Champagne sabayon is spooned over fresh berries and glazed the same way, which makes a gratin of fruit. Zabaglione is served warm in a glass with biscuits, or whisked cold and folded with cream. Whisk warm butter into an unsweetened foam and it becomes a hollandaise, which has its own entry.

Scrambled: too much heat, or the whisk stopped, and the edges set into flecks. Lift it off the heat the moment it reaches the ribbon; strain a lightly flecked sabayon, and start a scrambled one again. Thin and collapsing: it came off before the ribbon, so the yolks never set enough to hold the air; return it to the heat and keep whisking. Sinking on the plate: it stood too long, so make it as the plate is called, or whisk it cold and fold in whipped cream. Tasting raw and eggy: undercooked.

For the guest, a sabayon is a warm wine custard foam, light and fragrant. With Champagne over berries it tastes like a warm, airy custard with the lift of the wine; over oysters or fish it is savoury and glazed golden. Say it sah-bah-YOHN, and zabaglione zah-bahl-YOH-nay. The wine is only lightly cooked in the whisking, so tell a guest who avoids alcohol that it is made with wine. Yolks and wine are its base, and allergy questions go to the kitchen.

cards.back: Without sugar, with Champagne, a wine reduction or stock; spooned over fish or oysters and glazed golden under the salamander.

cards.front: What does a sabayon have to do with hollandaise?
cards.back: The same yolk foam, whisked over heat to a ribbon, is the first stage of a hollandaise; warm butter whisked into an unsweetened foam makes the sauce.

cards.front: What is a gratin of fruit?
cards.back: Fresh fruit, often berries, covered with a Champagne sabayon and glazed under the salamander until it browns in patches.

cards.front: Why must a warm sabayon be served as soon as it is made?
cards.back: A warm foam slowly loses its air and sinks; make it as the plate is called, or whisk it cold and fold in whipped cream.

cards.front: What should a server tell a guest who avoids alcohol about sabayon?
cards.back: That it is made with wine, which is only lightly cooked in the whisking, so the alcohol is not cooked away.

cards.front: Why use a round-bottomed bowl for sabayon?
cards.back: The whisk reaches every part of it, so no egg sits unstirred in a corner and scrambles while the rest is still thin.

questions.q: Which wine goes into a classic Italian zabaglione?
questions.answer: Marsala
distractors: Sauternes
Port
Madeira
questions.why: Zabaglione, the Italian original of sabayon, is made with Marsala, the fortified wine of Sicily; French cooks often use Champagne or sweet white wine.

questions.q: Which is a working ratio for sabayon, for each person?
questions.answer: 1 yolk, about 25 g sugar, 30 to 50 ml wine
distractors: 3 whole eggs, 100 g sugar, 250 ml wine
1 yolk, 100 g butter, 30 ml lemon juice
2 whites, 50 g sugar, no wine at all
questions.why: One yolk a person, sweetened and loosened with a little wine, gives a foam that rises well and holds; butter and lemon make a hollandaise instead.

questions.q: How does a cook know a sabayon is ready to come off the heat?
questions.answer: It falls from the whisk in a ribbon
distractors: It begins to boil at the edges
It turns clear and thin
It sets firm enough to slice when cold
questions.why: The ribbon shows the yolks have thickened enough to hold their air; any longer and they begin to scramble at the edges of the bowl.

questions.q: Why must the bowl of a sabayon never touch the simmering water?
questions.answer: Direct heat scrambles the yolks
distractors: The wine would evaporate at once
The sugar would crystallise
The bowl would crack in the heat
questions.why: Steam rising from barely simmering water warms the yolks gently; a bowl touching the water sets the egg on the bottom into curds.

questions.q: How does a savoury sabayon differ from a sweet one?
questions.answer: No sugar; Champagne or stock instead
distractors: It is set with gelatine and chilled
It is thickened with flour
It is made with whites, not yolks
questions.why: The method is the same; only the flavour changes, and the savoury foam is spooned over fish or oysters and glazed under the salamander.

questions.q: A sabayon is the same foam as the first stage of which sauce?
questions.answer: Hollandaise
distractors: Béchamel
Velouté
Espagnole
questions.why: Hollandaise starts with yolks whisked over heat to a ribbon, a sabayon, before the butter goes in; the other three are thickened with roux.

questions.q: Why is a warm sabayon made just before it is served?
questions.answer: It slowly loses its air and sinks
distractors: It turns bitter within seconds
It hardens into a set custard
The wine turns to vinegar
questions.why: A warm foam cannot hold its air for long; made as the plate is called, it reaches the guest light and tall.

questions.q: What is a gratin of fruit?
questions.answer: Berries under a glazed sabayon
distractors: Fruit baked in a pastry case
Fruit poached in red wine
Fruit set in a gelatine jelly
questions.why: The sabayon is spooned over the fruit and browned in patches under the salamander, so warm foam meets cool, sharp fruit.

entries.title: Pâte à choux
entries.summary: Pâte à choux is a paste of water or milk, butter, flour and eggs, cooked on the stove and baked until steam puffs it hollow. It makes éclairs, profiteroles, Paris-Brest, croquembouche and gougères and, fried, beignets soufflés.
entries.guest: Choux is the light, eggy pastry behind cream puffs and éclairs: crisp outside, hollow inside, and filled with cream or ice cream.

paras: Pâte à choux, cabbage paste, takes its name from the little round puffs it bakes into, which look like tiny cabbages. It is cooked twice, on the stove and then in the oven, and has no yeast, no layers of butter and no baking powder. It rises on steam alone. The water in the paste boils in the oven's heat, and the stretchy, egg-rich paste traps it and swells into a hollow shell that the egg then sets firm.
That hollow is the point: choux is a container for cream, ice cream or a savoury filling.

A classic batch is 250 ml (about 1 cup) of water or milk, 100 g (3.5 oz) of butter, 150 g (5 oz) of flour, a pinch each of salt and sugar, and four or five eggs. Milk gives a softer, browner shell, water a crisper one, and many kitchens use half and half. The egg is never a fixed number: eggs vary, and so does the water the paste lost on the stove, so the eggs go in gradually until the paste is right, by the house standard.

Bring the liquid, butter, salt and sugar to a full boil, so the butter has melted by the time the water boils. Off the heat, tip in all the flour at once and beat hard until it comes together. Stir it over medium heat for one to two minutes, until it pulls away from the sides in a smooth ball and leaves a thin film on the pan. This cooked paste is the panade. Drying it lets it take more egg, and more egg means a bigger puff.

Beat the panade briefly in a mixer to let the worst of the steam out, so the first egg does not cook. Beat in the eggs one at a time, each fully taken in before the next; the paste looks broken, then comes back glossy. Add the last egg beaten, a little at a time, and test: the paste should fall slowly from the spoon and leave a V-shaped point hanging from its edge, the dropping consistency.

Pipe onto lined trays, well spaced. Bake hot to puff, around 200 to 220°C (392 to 428°F), and keep the door shut for at least the first 15 minutes, because cool air before the walls have set collapses the shells. Once they are risen and golden, lower the oven to around 160 to 180°C (320 to 356°F) to dry the walls through. Many cooks then pierce each shell and return it briefly to let the steam out.

Profiteroles are small balls filled with cream or ice cream, often under chocolate sauce. Éclairs are piped fingers, filled and glazed with fondant or chocolate. The Paris-Brest is a ring scattered with almonds and filled with praline cream; by the usual account Louis Durand, a pastry cook of Maisons-Laffitte, made it in 1910 to honour the Paris-Brest-Paris bicycle race, and the ring recalls a wheel. The croquembouche is a tall cone of filled puffs held with caramel, a French celebration piece for weddings and christenings. Gougères are choux beaten with grated cheese, such as Gruyère, the savoury puff of Burgundy.

Fried, choux makes beignets soufflés: spoonfuls dropped into hot oil swell into light, hollow fritters. The New Orleans beignet, with its own entry, is another thing: a yeast dough, rolled and cut before frying.

Flat: too much egg, too cool an oven, or the door opened early; add the last egg gradually and test for the V. Collapsed after baking: underbaked, the walls had not set; bake longer at the lower heat until crisp and fully golden. Hollow but soggy inside: not dried; pierce the shells and return them to a low oven. Cracked and lopsided: the paste was too stiff, with too little egg.

To a guest, choux is the light, crisp pastry of cream puffs and éclairs. Shells are filled to order or close to service, because a filled shell softens as it stands. Say choux as SHOO, and pâte à choux as paht ah SHOO. It is made with flour, butter and eggs, so allergy and dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

cards.back: Steam alone: the water in the paste boils in a hot oven, and the stretchy egg paste traps it, swells, then sets hollow.

cards.back: Hot first, around 200 to 220°C (392 to 428°F), to puff, then cooler, around 160 to 180°C (320 to 356°F), to dry the walls.

cards.front: Choux shells came out flat. What are the likely causes?
cards.back: Too much egg made the paste too loose, the oven was too cool, or the door was opened before the shells had set.

Baking powder
Layers of butter

questions.q: How does a cook judge that enough egg has gone into choux paste?
questions.answer: It falls from the spoon leaving a V
distractors: It holds a stiff peak like meringue
It is firm enough to roll out
It runs off the spoon like cream
questions.why: A paste that falls slowly and leaves a V-shaped point is soft enough to puff yet firm enough to hold its piped shape.

questions.answer: To dry it so it takes more egg

To melt the sugar into a caramel
To cool it down more quickly
questions.why: Driving off some water lets the panade absorb more egg, and the egg is what stretches around the steam and sets the shell.

distractors: It keeps the butter from melting out
It stops the tops from cracking
It lets the sugar caramelise evenly
questions.why: The shells are held up by steam until the egg sets their walls; a rush of cool air too soon and they fall.

questions.q: A tray of choux has spread flat in the oven. What is the likely cause?
questions.answer: Too much egg, or too cool an oven
distractors: Too little sugar in the paste
Too long in the drying oven
Piping onto a tray lined with parchment
questions.why: A loose paste spreads before it can puff, and a cool oven makes steam too slowly to lift it before it settles.

questions.answer: Pierce them and dry them in a low oven

Brush them with egg and bake hotter
Chill them overnight to firm up
questions.why: Steam trapped inside softens the walls; letting it out and drying the shells in a low oven leaves them crisp right through.

It is made with no flour

questions.why: Beignets soufflés are spoonfuls of fried choux; the New Orleans beignet is a yeast dough rolled and cut into squares, then fried.

entries.title: Meringues: French, Swiss and Italian
entries.summary: Egg white whipped with sugar into a glossy foam, made three ways: French with raw whites, Swiss warmed over a bain-marie, a bowl set over simmering water, and Italian with hot syrup. Each has its strengths and faults, and all three need a clean bowl.
entries.guest: Meringue is egg white whipped with sugar until glossy. On our Lemon Tart it is piped and toasted, soft and marshmallowy, against the sharp yuzu mousse and lemon jelly.

paras: A meringue is egg white whipped with sugar into a glossy foam that holds its shape. Whipping unfolds the proteins in the white, and they knit into a thin film around each air bubble; the sugar dissolves into that film and makes it thicker, glossier and slower to collapse. Baked low and long, a meringue dries crisp; toasted, it browns like a marshmallow; folded in, it lightens a mousse or a soufflé.

There are three methods, and they differ in how much heat the whites meet. French uses raw whites and is the lightest and least stable. Swiss warms the whites and sugar together before whipping. Italian cooks the whites with hot syrup and is the most stable.

French: whip the whites in a spotless bowl to soft peaks, then add the sugar a spoonful at a time, whipping well between each, until stiff, glossy and no longer gritty between the fingers. Sugar added too early slows the foam; added all at once, it knocks it flat. Dry it in a cool oven, about 90 to 100°C (194 to 212°F), for one and a half to two hours.

Swiss: whisk the whites and sugar in a bowl over simmering water until the sugar dissolves and the mix reaches 60 to 70°C (140 to 158°F), then whip off the heat until thick, glossy and cool. It is denser and silkier than French and pipes cleanly.

Italian: boil sugar with about a third of its weight in water to 118 to 121°C (244 to 250°F), firm ball to the very start of hard ball, while the whites whip to soft peaks. Pour the syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl, mixer running, never onto the whisk, and whip until barely warm. The syrup partly cooks the whites, so the foam holds for hours, needs no baking and stands up to butter in buttercream.

Most meringues use about twice the weight of sugar to white: 200 g (7 oz) of sugar to 100 g (3.5 oz) of white, roughly three large whites. That bakes crisp and holds; a soft topping can drop towards equal weights. Cream of tartar, a fine acid powder left over from winemaking, about 1 g for each 100 g of white, steadies a French meringue.

Read the peaks by lifting the whisk. Soft peaks slump over at once; firm peaks hold, the tip curling like a wave; stiff peaks stand straight up. Soft peaks suit folding, stiff peaks piping and baking.

French meringue makes crisp shells, the poached spoonfuls of œufs à la neige (snow eggs, floated on crème anglaise and now often called île flottante), the vacherin (a ring of crisp meringue filled with cream or ice cream) and, folded in, soufflés. A pavlova adds cornflour and vinegar for a crisp shell over a soft centre. The cooked meringues, Italian above all, make toasted tops for tarts, baked Alaska, where the foam shields cold ice cream from a hot oven, and buttercream.

Fat is the enemy. A trace of yolk, a greasy bowl or a plastic bowl holding old fat stops the whites foaming, because fat gets between the proteins and keeps them from forming their film. Separate each egg over a small bowl, so one broken yolk spoils one white, and wipe the bowl and whisk with lemon juice first.

Whites whipped past stiff turn dry and lumpy and will weep: a fresh white whisked in saves them for folding, but not for piping. Beads of syrup on a baked meringue mean undissolved sugar or too hot an oven. A topping that pools liquid underneath was not cooked through below.

On the Lemon Tart the meringue is piped and toasted, so its peaks caramelise into a crisp shell over a soft, marshmallow centre, sweet against the yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and sweet pastry crumb. Italian and Swiss meringues, being cooked, hold their shape on a plate and can be browned with a torch; which of the two the pastry kitchen makes, and how it browns it, is a question for the chef.

Keep it plain at the table: egg white whipped with sugar, piped and toasted. The Lemon Tart is the lightest dessert, the one to offer after a rich meal. Any egg or allergy question goes to the kitchen and the service note, never an answer from memory.

entries.title: Caramel and the sugar stages
entries.summary: Sugar boiled through its named stages, from thread to hard crack and into caramel, read by thermometer and by colour. It can be made dry or wet, is stopped with warm cream and runs through Brennan's desserts, from the Foster to the bread pudding.
entries.guest: Caramel is sugar cooked until it turns amber and nutty. On our bread pudding it becomes a whiskey caramel, and in The Snickers a silky caramel custard.

paras: As a sugar syrup boils, water leaves it and the temperature climbs; the hotter it gets, the less water is left and the harder the sugar sets as it cools. Pastry cooks name those points as stages. Once almost all the water has gone, from about 160°C (320°F), the sugar itself begins to break down and brown: that is caramel, and with the colour come new flavours, nutty and toasty, then bitter. Each stage is a tool: thread for syrups and glazes, soft ball for fudge and pralines, firm ball for Italian meringue, hard ball for nougat and marshmallow, soft crack for butterscotch, hard crack for spun sugar, caramel for sauces and custards.

Read the stages with a sugar thermometer, or drop a little syrup into cold water. Thread, 106 to 112°C (223 to 234°F), falls in a fine thread. Soft ball, 112 to 116°C (234 to 241°F), makes a ball that flattens in the hand. Firm ball, 118 to 120°C (244 to 248°F), holds but gives. Hard ball, 121 to 130°C (250 to 266°F), holds firm. Soft crack, 132 to 143°C (270 to 289°F), sets hard but bends. Hard crack, 149 to 154°C (300 to 309°F), snaps clean. Authors draw the lines a degree or two apart, so follow the recipe in hand.

A wet caramel starts with sugar and about a third of its weight in water, stirred over medium heat until dissolved. Once it boils, stop stirring: swirl the pan, and wash crystals from the sides with a wet pastry brush. A spoonful of glucose or a few drops of lemon juice guards against crystallising, because they get in the way of the sugar re-forming into grains. A dry caramel is sugar alone, spread in a heavy pan and melted from the edges inward, swirled as it liquefies: quicker, deeper in flavour and easier to scorch.

Past 160°C (320°F), read the colour: pale straw, golden, then amber at about 170 to 180°C (338 to 356°F), then mahogany. Amber suits most sauces and custards. Past deep amber the sugar turns bitter within seconds, and the hot pan carries it on after it leaves the flame, so take it off a shade early.

To stop a caramel, take it off the heat and add warm cream or butter in stages, or dip the base of the pan in cold water. Cream boils up hard and throws scalding steam, so stand back, keep your face and arms clear and use a long whisk. Caramel is far hotter than boiling water and clings to skin: never taste it from the spoon, cool any burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, never ice, and tell the chef.

A caramel sauce is amber caramel loosened with cream and a little butter and salt, about equal weights of sugar and cream. Crème caramel is a custard baked in a mould lined with caramel, which melts into a thin sauce as it rests and floods the plate when the custard is turned out. Praline is nuts set in caramel, then crushed or ground; nougatine is caramel with flaked almonds, rolled thin while warm and cut or shaped.

A syrup that clouds and turns sandy was stirred after it boiled, or seeded by a crystal on the side of the pan: add water, dissolve it and begin again. A dry caramel that burns in patches was heated too fast or not swirled. Caramel that seizes into lumps met cold cream: stir it over low heat until smooth. Black, bitter caramel cannot be saved.

Caramel runs through the dessert menu. Bananas Foster begins with butter, brown sugar and cinnamon bubbled to a blond caramel, kept light so it does not set into toffee on the cold ice cream. The New Orleans Bread Pudding carries a whiskey caramel, amber caramel loosened with cream and butter, the whiskey bringing vanilla and oak. The Snickers has a caramel custard, kin to crème caramel. On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, charring drives water from the pineapple and caramelises its sugars. Which whiskey goes into the caramel is a question for the chef, and guests who avoid alcohol are told it carries whiskey.

entries.title: Bananas Foster
entries.summary: Bananas turned in a caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, loosened with banana liqueur, flamed with dark rum and spooned warm over vanilla ice cream. The fruit must be ripe but firm and the caramel smooth and blond before the rum is lit.
entries.guest: Bananas Foster is bananas cooked in a caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, flamed with rum and spooned warm over our housemade vanilla ice cream.

paras: Bananas Foster is a pan dessert built in minutes: butter, brown sugar and cinnamon melted into a bubbling caramel, banana liqueur to loosen it, bananas turned until just soft, then dark rum added and set alight. Fruit and sauce, glossy and buttery, are spooned warm over cold vanilla ice cream, so hot meets cold in every spoonful. Each step has a reason, and a cook who knows them makes it the same way every time, in the kitchen or at the guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), the tableside cart.

The proportions are simple: one banana a person, about three times as much brown sugar as butter by weight, a pinch of cinnamon, and banana liqueur and rum in equal measure. At Brennan's, follow the house procedure you are trained on rather than any recipe found elsewhere, and never quote quantities to a guest.

Melt the butter in a wide pan over medium heat, add the brown sugar and cinnamon, and stir until the sugar has dissolved and the mixture bubbles into a smooth, blond caramel, the butter held in the sauce rather than floating on it. Stir in the banana liqueur. Cut each banana in half lengthwise, then across, so the pieces lie flat.

Lay the bananas in the caramel and cook until they begin to soften, a minute or two, then turn them once and spoon the sauce over. Take the pan off the flame, add the measured rum, return it and tilt the far edge towards the flame to light it, away from you and the guests; the flame technique and its rules have their own entries. Baste as the flame burns out and the caramel deepens. Lay the bananas over the ice cream, then pour the warm sauce over them.

Choose bananas ripe but firm: fully yellow, sweet and fragrant, with few or no brown spots. Underripe fruit tastes starchy and stays hard; a soft, speckled banana is sweeter but collapses into purée in the hot caramel. The pan only warms the fruit and softens its outside, so the banana must arrive sweet and firm.

Get the caramel smooth before the fruit goes in. The cool bananas and their juice drop the heat, so undissolved sugar stays as grit, and a split caramel, butter pooling on top, will not come back together around the fruit. If it splits, take it off the heat and whisk in a spoonful of liqueur or water until glossy.

The rum must be warm enough to light. What burns is alcohol vapour, not the liquid, and cold rum in a pan that has cooled gives off too little to catch; a hot pan warms it in seconds. A flame that will not take is never chased with more spirit from the bottle.

The Foster belongs to the flamed fruit desserts. Cherries jubilee, generally credited to Escoffier, is cherries in syrup lit with spirit. The house guide also prints a Cherries Jubilee, tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce flamed over the same housemade vanilla ice cream, but it is not on the current dessert menu: confirm with a manager before offering it. Crêpes Suzette are thin pancakes warmed in an orange butter sauce and flamed with orange liqueur. Behind them stand the caramelised bananas of home kitchens, fried in butter and brown sugar, where the Foster began.

World Famous Bananas Foster is on the menu at every meal, made at the table for two or more. The house keeps the caramel blond and bubbling and turns ripe but firm bananas, halved and quartered, just once. The menu prints rum; the house's published recipe adds banana liqueur, which loosens the caramel and deepens the banana flavour, while dark rum brings molasses, spice and the strength to catch. Which rum the kitchen pours is a question for the chef. The vanilla ice cream is made in house.

The story and the cart belong to Bananas Foster at the table. Flaming burns the vapour above the pan, not all the alcohol in it, so much of the rum and liqueur stays in the sauce: tell any guest who avoids alcohol, and steer them to the Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin. Send every question about what is in the ice cream to the kitchen.

entries.title: New Orleans bread pudding
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans bread pudding.
entries.summary: Stale French bread soaked in a sweet, spiced custard and baked until just set, served warm with a whiskey sauce. A thrift dish New Orleans made its own, because the city's light bread drinks custard without turning to paste.
entries.guest: Our bread pudding is served warm with a whiskey caramel, tangy buttermilk ice cream and pralines, the New Orleans pecan candy, for crunch.

paras: Bread pudding is stale bread given a second life. The bread is torn or cubed, soaked in a custard of milk or cream, eggs, sugar, vanilla and spice, often with raisins, then baked until the custard sets around it. The top crisps and browns; inside it is soft, sweet and custardy, closer to a baked custard than to bread. It began as a European way to use up bread, and in New Orleans it became a staple, served warm with a sauce, usually whiskey.

Recipes vary, so follow the house recipe in hand. A sound starting point is about 450 g (1 lb) of day-old French bread to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of milk, or milk and cream, with 4 to 6 eggs, 150 to 250 g (5 to 9 oz) of sugar, vanilla, cinnamon, nutmeg and a handful of raisins. More cream makes it richer and softer; more egg makes it firmer. The test is the soak: the bread saturated, but not swimming.

Tear or cube the bread, crust and all, into a buttered dish, with the raisins scattered through. Whisk the eggs and sugar, then the milk, vanilla and spice, and pour the custard over. Press the bread down so it drinks, and rest it for 20 to 30 minutes, or covered overnight in the fridge, pressing once or twice. The rest lets the custard reach the centre of every piece, so no dry cores bake through.
Bake at about 175°C (347°F) for 45 minutes to an hour, until puffed, golden and set. A water bath, the dish set in a tray of hot water, gives gentler heat and a smoother custard.

New Orleans French bread suits it because of its crumb: light, airy and thin crusted, with little fat or sugar of its own. It stales within a day, and stale bread has dried enough to soak up a great deal of custard while keeping its shape. A dense or rich loaf drinks slowly and bakes heavy; fresh bread turns to paste.

It is done when it is set at the centre: a knife pushed in near the middle comes out clean, and only the very middle wobbles when the dish is nudged. A probe there reads about 71 to 77°C (160 to 171°F). Underbaked, it is wet and eggy inside. Baked too long or too hot, the custard curdles, weeping liquid and turning grainy and dry. A pool of custard under the bread means too much liquid or too short a soak.

Whiskey sauce is the classic partner: butter and sugar melted together, bound with a beaten egg or with cream, finished with bourbon and poured warm. A typical proportion is 115 g (4 oz) of butter, 200 g (7 oz) of sugar, one egg and 30 to 60 ml (2 to 4 tbsp) of bourbon. Whisk a little of the hot butter and sugar into the egg, return it and whisk off the heat until it thickens, then add the bourbon. Too hot, and the egg scrambles and the sauce splits; a sauce bound with cream holds better.

Bread pudding has been in New Orleans cookbooks since the nineteenth century, and the Picayune's Creole Cook Book, in its 1901 edition, already prints one. The city's French bread stales fast, and nothing went to waste. The warm whiskey sauce came later: restaurants revived the dessert from the 1970s with whiskey and bourbon sauces, and it is now the signature.

At Brennan's the New Orleans Bread Pudding comes with a whiskey caramel rather than the classic sauce: amber caramel loosened with cream and butter, with whiskey for vanilla and oak, steadier in service than a sauce bound with egg. Buttermilk ice cream brings a gentle tang that cools the warm pudding and cuts the sweetness, and pralines add crunch. Which whiskey the kitchen uses is a question for the chef, and ask the kitchen before saying whether the pralines are made in house.

Describe it warmly and plainly: soft, custardy bread pudding, whiskey caramel, tangy ice cream and pralines for crunch. Tell anyone who avoids alcohol that the caramel carries whiskey. Every question about eggs, nuts or anything else in the dish goes to the kitchen and the service note.

entries.title: Pain perdu
entries.summary: Pain perdu, lost bread, is stale bread soaked in a sweet custard of egg, milk, sugar and spice, then fried in butter until golden outside and just set within. It is the Creole name for French toast, and an old New Orleans breakfast.
entries.guest: Pain perdu means lost bread: thick slices soaked in a sweet egg custard and cooked until golden. Ours is made from our own citrus brioche, with mascarpone mousse, raspberry coulis and fresh local raspberries.

paras: Pain perdu is French for lost bread: the loaf that would be lost to the bin once it goes stale. Instead the cook slices it thick, soaks it in a custard of egg, milk, sugar and spice, and fries it in butter. The dry crumb drinks the custard like a sponge, and the pan turns the outside golden and crisp while the inside sets soft, rather like a baked custard.

Stale bread works better than fresh. Fresh bread is already soft and moist, so it soaks to mush and tears; a day or two old, it takes up custard and still holds its shape. Cooks across Europe have saved old bread this way for centuries. In New Orleans it was a Creole breakfast under its French name, and many locals still call it pain perdu rather than French toast, eaten with cane syrup poured over or simply dusted with icing sugar.

A dependable custard is 4 large eggs to 250 ml (about 1 cup) of milk, or milk and cream, with 25 g (2 tbsp) of sugar, a pinch of salt, vanilla and a little cinnamon or nutmeg. That soaks about six thick slices. More egg gives a firmer, eggier set; more cream a richer, softer one. Whisk until no streaks of white remain, or the toast comes out patched with fried egg white.

Soak by the bread, not by the clock. Light New Orleans French bread, airy under a thin crust, needs only a few seconds a side before it starts to fall apart. Dense, rich brioche takes longer, 20 to 30 seconds a side, and a thick, dry slice can sit for a minute or more. The slice is ready when it feels heavy and soaked to the middle but still holds together when lifted. Let the excess drip off before it goes into the pan.

Cook over medium heat in foaming butter, about 2 to 3 minutes a side, until each face is a deep golden brown. The heat is a balance: too high and the sugar in the custard burns before the centre sets; too low and the bread stews in the butter and turns greasy. Slices thicker than about 2.5 cm (1 inch) are browned in the pan, then finished in an oven at 175°C (347°F) for 5 to 8 minutes, until the centre is hot and set with no wet custard. The US food safety charts give 71°C (160°F) for egg dishes.

Most faults come from the soak or the heat. A wet, raw middle means the slice soaked too long for its bread, or browned before the custard inside could set: lower the heat and finish thick slices in the oven. Burnt outside and raw inside is a pan too hot. Pale and greasy is a pan too cool, or butter not yet foaming. Torn slices mean bread too fresh or cut too thin.

At Brennan's the pain perdu is the Framboise French Toast, framboise being French for raspberry. The kitchen bakes its own citrus brioche, a bread rich with egg and butter and scented with zest, and slices it thick so it soaks up custard without falling apart. It is finished with a mascarpone mousse, mascarpone (mas-kar-POH-nay) being a rich, mild Italian fresh cheese, here whipped light; a raspberry coulis (koo-LEE), a smooth fruit sauce pushed through a sieve; and fresh local raspberries. The children's breakfast offers a simpler vanilla French toast with fresh berries and whipped cream.

The Framboise French Toast sits among the starters, so a guest may not expect a sweet plate: say sweet when you describe it, and offer it for the table to share or as a sweet course to finish. Say framboise as frahm-BWAHZ. For a guest who wants no wine, the guide's pairing is our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory, which balances the sweetness. For the children's plate, remind parents that the set breakfast also opens with fruit and ends with ice cream. Questions about what goes into either plate go to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Beignets
entries.summary: New Orleans beignets are squares of rich yeast dough fried until they puff hollow, then buried in icing sugar and eaten hot. Café du Monde, a French Market coffee stand since 1862, serves them with café au lait, and visitors often ask about them.
entries.guest: Beignets are the New Orleans doughnut: squares of light yeast dough fried until puffed and hollow, then served hot under a heap of icing sugar.

paras: Beignet is French for a fritter: something made of dough or batter and fried. In New Orleans the word means one thing above all, a square of rich yeast dough fried until it puffs into a hollow pillow, then buried under icing sugar and eaten hot. It is closer to a doughnut than to a pastry, with no hole and no glaze, and it is at its best within minutes of leaving the oil, while the sugar still clings to the warm crust.

The puff is the point. When the dough meets hot oil, the water in it turns to steam and the gas the yeast has made expands, so the square balloons and leaves a hollow at its centre. A good beignet is crisp and golden outside, soft and a little chewy within, and light enough to eat three at a sitting.

The dough is an enriched yeast dough: flour, milk, egg, butter or shortening, sugar, salt and yeast. A useful proportion is 500 g (about 4 cups) of flour to about 300 ml (1 1/4 cups) of milk, 1 egg, 50 g (1/4 cup) of sugar, 40 g (3 tbsp) of butter, 7 g (1/4 oz) of instant yeast and 8 g (1 1/2 tsp) of salt, mixed to a soft, slightly sticky dough and kneaded until smooth. Some recipes use evaporated milk for a richer, more tender crumb.

Let it rise until roughly doubled, about an hour in a warm kitchen, or overnight in the fridge, where the dough firms and rolls more easily. Roll it about 3 to 5 mm (1/8 to 1/4 inch) thick and cut it into squares of about 5 to 7.5 cm (2 to 3 inches) with a knife or a pastry wheel. Squares leave no scraps, and rerolled scraps fry tough. Rest the squares 10 to 15 minutes under a cloth so the dough relaxes and they puff evenly.

Fry a few at a time at 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F), turning once, about a minute a side, until puffed and golden. Drain them on a rack and shower them with icing sugar at once, while they are hot. The frying entry covers the oil, the thermometer and the fry station.

Flat, dense beignets come from dough that was underproofed, rolled too thick, or fried in oil too cool to raise steam quickly. Greasy ones sat in oil below temperature, usually because too many went in at once. Dark outside and doughy inside means oil too hot. Lopsided ones were not rested after cutting, or not turned. And any beignet left waiting turns heavy, its sugar damp: fry to order.

Two cousins share the pot. Choux beignets, also called beignets soufflés, are spoonfuls of choux paste, the cooked egg dough of éclairs, fried until they swell; steam alone raises them, with no yeast. The Creole calas are rice fritters: cooked rice mixed with egg, sugar and flour, often raised with yeast, fried in spoonfuls and dusted with sugar. In French cooking at large, a beignet is any fritter, sweet or savoury, from apple rings in batter to vegetables.

Where the New Orleans beignet came from is told many ways, and each is a story rather than a record. One says French settlers brought the fritter in the eighteenth century; another credits the Ursuline nuns, who arrived in 1727; a third gives it to the Acadians, the French exiles from Canada who became the Cajuns. Tell them as stories. What is on record is the coffee stand: Café du Monde opened in the French Market in 1862 and still serves beignets with café au lait, half coffee and half hot milk.

Say ben-YAY. Beignets are not among the dishes in Brennan's house guide, so check the day's menu before you answer a guest who asks. Visitors usually want the French Market ritual: beignets hot from the fryer with a café au lait made from the city's coffee with chicory, eaten at once, sugar and all. Warn a guest in dark clothes about the sugar: it goes everywhere.

entries.title: Pralines
entries.summary: New Orleans pralines are pecan sweets of white and brown sugar, butter and cream, cooked to the soft ball, beaten until creamy and spooned into rounds that set soft like fudge. They descend from a French sugared almond, remade by the city's Creole cooks.
entries.guest: Pralines are the New Orleans pecan candy: brown sugar, butter and cream cooked with pecans until creamy. On our bread pudding they add crunch and caramel sweetness.

paras: A New Orleans praline is a flat, round sweet of pecans set in a creamy, fudge-like sugar: white and brown sugar, butter and cream or milk, cooked together, beaten and spooned out to set. It breaks cleanly, then melts on the tongue with a fine, slightly sandy grain. That grain is the craft: the cook decides, by heat and by beating, how large the sugar crystals grow.

The French praline is a different sweet with the same name: almonds or hazelnuts coated in caramelised sugar, hard and crunchy, which French pastry crushes into pralin or grinds into praliné paste. New Orleans kept the name, used the pecans that grew all around it and added cream, turning a hard sugared nut into a soft patty. Say PRAH-leen, never PRAY-leen.

A home batch uses about equal weights of white and light brown sugar, around 400 g (14 oz) in all, with 120 ml (1/2 cup) of cream or evaporated milk, 55 g (4 tbsp) of butter, 150 g (1 1/2 cups) of pecan halves, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of vanilla. Toasting the pecans first deepens their flavour.

Bring the sugars, cream and butter to the boil in a heavy pan, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then keep stirring gently, scraping the base so the cream does not catch, and cook to the soft ball, 112 to 116°C (234 to 241°F). Without a thermometer, drop a little into cold water: it forms a soft ball that flattens when lifted out. The caramel entry covers the sugar stages in full.

Take the pan off the heat, stir in the vanilla and pecans, and beat with a wooden spoon. For a minute or two nothing seems to happen; then the gloss dulls, the syrup thickens and turns cloudy, and it begins to hold on the spoon. That is the moment. Spoon it at once onto baking parchment or buttered marble in rounds of about 5 to 7.5 cm (2 to 3 inches), working fast, because it sets in the pot within a minute or two. The pralines firm in 15 to 30 minutes.

Beating is a race. Spooned too soon, the mixture spreads into thin, glossy puddles that stay sticky. Beaten too long, it seizes in the pot and turns crumbly: stir in a spoonful of hot milk or water over low heat and spoon again. Undercooked syrup never sets; overcooked syrup sets hard and sugary. Weather matters too. Sugar draws water from the air, so on a humid day pralines can stay soft and tacky; cooks take the syrup a degree or two higher, or wait for a dry day.

The praline is named for César, duc de Choiseul, comte du Plessis-Praslin, a seventeenth-century French marshal and diplomat; by tradition his cook first sugared almonds, though the story may be legend. Tradition credits the Ursuline nuns, who came to New Orleans in 1727, with bringing the recipe. Louisiana cooks swapped in pecans and added milk or cream, and many accounts credit the city's Black cooks, enslaved and free, with that change. In the nineteenth century women called pralinières, many of them free women of colour, sold pralines in the streets of the French Quarter. Popular accounts say some enslaved sellers saved their earnings towards freedom; tell that as an account, not a record.

At Brennan's, pralines crown the New Orleans Bread Pudding, crumbled over the warm pudding with its whiskey caramel and buttermilk ice cream. They bring crunch and a caramel sweetness against the soft custard and the tang of the ice cream. Whether they are made in house is not public, so ask the kitchen before calling them housemade.

Locals say PRAH-leen; if a guest says PRAY-leen, never correct them, and keep saying PRAH-leen yourself. When a guest asks about the history, credit the pralinières, the women, many of them free women of colour, who sold pralines in the French Quarter streets and made them part of the city's life. Pralines are made with pecans, butter and cream, so nut and dairy questions go to the service note and the kitchen, never a verdict from you.

entries.title: Bavarian cream
entries.say: As it reads: Bavarian cream, or bavarois, bah-vahr-WAH.
entries.summary: Bavarian cream, bavarois in French, is crème anglaise set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, then chilled in a mould and turned out. Silky and light yet able to stand, it sits between a mousse and a custard.
entries.guest: A Bavarian cream is a light, set cream, somewhere between a mousse and a custard. In our Snickers it is milk chocolate, with caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts.

paras: A Bavarian cream, bavarois in French, is three things folded into one: a crème anglaise, the stirred pouring custard of milk, sugar and yolks; gelatine, which sets it; and whipped cream, which lightens it. The mixture is poured into a mould, chilled until firm and turned out to stand on the plate with a clean shape.

It sits between a mousse and a custard: the custard base and the gelatine let it hold a mould where a mousse could not, while the whipped cream keeps it lighter than any custard. Gelatine melts at about 35°C (95°F), below the warmth of the mouth, so a good bavarois dissolves on the tongue.

A common working ratio is 8 to 10 g of leaf gelatine for each 500 ml (about 2 cups) of anglaise, with roughly an equal volume of lightly whipped cream. Sheets differ in weight and strength by grade, so weigh the gelatine rather than counting leaves. A tall mould, a warm room or a fruit base wants the top of that range; a cream served in a glass can take less, and the house recipe has the last word.

Soak the gelatine leaves in plenty of cold water for 5 to 10 minutes until soft, then squeeze them out. Make a crème anglaise, cooked to 82 to 84°C (180 to 183°F), when it coats the spoon; its own entry teaches the method. Off the heat, stir the squeezed gelatine into the hot custard until it dissolves, then strain. Chocolate, coffee or praline paste goes in now, while it is hot.

Cool the custard over iced water, stirring, until it starts to thicken like unbeaten egg white, at roughly 20 to 25°C (68 to 77°F). This is the moment to fold. Stir in a third of the whipped cream to loosen it, then fold in the rest gently with a spatula until no streaks remain. Pour into a mould rinsed with cold water or lightly oiled, and chill for at least 4 hours, until firm. To turn it out, dip the mould in warm water for a few seconds, loosen the edge and invert it onto the plate.

The fold is where a bavarois is won or lost. Folded too warm, the custard melts the cream, which collapses, and the mixture separates into a dense jelly below and foam above. Folded too late, the custard has already set in lumps and leaves rubbery streaks: warm it over hot water until just melted, cool it again and fold. Overwhipped cream turns grainy and will not fold smoothly, so whip only to soft peaks. Fresh pineapple, kiwi, papaya and figs carry enzymes that break gelatine down, so they are cooked first.

Flavour the custard and the family grows: vanilla is the classic, with chocolate, coffee, praline and liqueurs beside it. A fruit bavarois replaces some or all of the custard with a sweetened fruit purée, set and lightened the same way. Two grand moulded desserts are built from it: the charlotte russe, a mould lined with sponge fingers and filled with bavarois, and the charlotte royale, lined with slices of jam-filled Swiss roll.

Carême, the Paris pastry cook of the early nineteenth century, gave the bavarois its classic form, and Escoffier's Guide Culinaire later set out a whole family of them. Why it is named for Bavaria is unclear, so tell no story of it as fact.

At Brennan's the bavarois is the chocolate of The Snickers, the pastry kitchen's candy bar taken apart and rebuilt: a milk chocolate Bavarian cream beside caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts. The menu prints Bavarian milk chocolate, which almost certainly means a milk chocolate Bavarian cream rather than chocolate from Bavaria; confirm at lineup. Never name a chocolate brand: none is confirmed.

Describe it as a light, set cream, between a mousse and a custard. Bavarian creams are usually set with gelatine, so a guest who avoids it, or eats vegetarian, needs a word with the kitchen before ordering; whether ours is set with gelatine is a lineup question, never a guess. The Snickers carries peanuts, printed in capitals in the guide: name them to every table before ordering, and send dietary questions to the kitchen.

cards.front: What three things make a Bavarian cream?
cards.back: Crème anglaise for the base, gelatine to set it and whipped cream to lighten it, chilled in a mould and turned out.

cards.front: Why is a bavarois said to sit between a mousse and a custard?

cards.front: Why weigh gelatine rather than count the leaves?
cards.back: Sheets differ in weight and strength by grade, so the same count can set one batch firm and leave another soft.

cards.front: When does the gelatine go into a bavarois?

cards.front: When is the whipped cream folded into the custard?

steps.title: Stir a crème anglaise
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a crème anglaise in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Bring the milk to a simmer with half the sugar and a split vanilla pod, then leave it off the heat to infuse
While the milk infuses, whisk the yolks with the rest of the sugar until pale
Pour about a third of the hot milk onto the yolks, whisking all the while, to temper them
Pour the tempered yolks back into the pan
Stir over low to medium heat in a figure of eight, reaching into the corners
Take it to 82 to 84°C (180 to 183°F), when it coats the spoon and a finger leaves a clean line
Strain it at once through a fine sieve into a cold bowl set over ice
Stir it now and then as it cools, then cover and chill
steps.distractor: Let it boil for a minute so the yolks thicken it fully
steps.why: The milk infuses first and the yolks are tempered before they go back into the pan. An anglaise is stirred only to nappe and never boiled, because a boil curdles the yolks; it goes straight into a cold bowl to stop the cooking.

steps.title: Cook a crème pâtissière
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a crème pâtissière in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Bring the milk to the boil with about half the sugar and a split vanilla pod
While the milk comes to the boil, whisk the yolks with the rest of the sugar, then whisk in the starch until smooth
Pour about a third of the hot milk onto the yolks, whisking, then return everything to the pan
Whisk over medium heat into the corners, and keep whisking through the lumpy stage
Once big, slow bubbles break the surface, keep whisking at the boil for one to two minutes
Off the heat, whisk in the butter
Spread it thinly in a lined tray, press cling film onto the surface and chill it quickly
Before use, beat it briefly until smooth, and stop there
steps.distractor: Take it off the heat at 82°C (180°F), before it can boil
steps.why: Pastry cream is the custard that must boil. One to two minutes at the boil swells the starch and destroys amylase, the yolk enzyme that would thin it overnight. Cling film on the surface stops a skin, and brief beating restores it without thinning it.

steps.title: Make pâte à choux
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a pâte à choux in order, from the pan to the oven. One stage does not belong.
steps: Bring the liquid, butter, salt and sugar to a full boil
Off the heat, tip in all the flour at once and beat until it comes together
Stir the panade over medium heat until it leaves a thin film on the pan
Beat it briefly in the mixer to let the worst of the steam out
Beat in the eggs one at a time, each fully taken in before the next
Add the last egg a little at a time, until the paste falls from the spoon in a V
Pipe it onto lined trays, well spaced
Bake hot, 200 to 220°C (392 to 428°F), with the door shut until the shells have set
Lower the oven to dry the walls through, then pierce the shells to let the steam out
steps.distractor: Beat in baking powder so the shells rise higher
steps.why: Choux rises on steam alone, with no baking powder. The panade is dried so it takes more egg, the eggs go in gradually to the V, then a hot oven puffs the shells and a cooler one dries them so they do not collapse.

steps.title: Make an Italian meringue
steps.prompt: Put the stages of an Italian meringue in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Boil the sugar with about a third of its weight in water
As the syrup climbs, whip the whites to soft peaks in a bowl wiped clean of any fat
Take the syrup off at 118 to 121°C (244 to 250°F), firm ball to the start of hard ball
With the mixer running, pour the syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl
Whip on until the meringue is thick, glossy and barely warm
Use it unbaked: pipe it and toast it with a torch, or beat it into buttercream
steps.distractor: Pour the syrup straight onto the spinning whisk so it mixes in faster
steps.why: The whites reach soft peaks in a fat-free bowl just as the syrup reaches firm ball, and the syrup goes down the side, never onto the whisk, where it spins into hard threads. Partly cooked, the foam needs no baking.

steps.title: Take a dry caramel to amber
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a dry caramel in order, from the bare pan to the stopped sauce. One stage does not belong.
steps: Warm the cream and set it beside the stove before the sugar goes on
Spread the sugar in an even layer in a clean, heavy pan
Melt it over medium heat until the edges begin to liquefy
Swirl the pan so the melted sugar draws in the dry and colours evenly
Keep swirling as it passes from pale straw to golden
Take it off the heat a shade early, as it turns amber at about 170 to 180°C (338 to 356°F)
Stand back and whisk in the warm cream in stages with a long whisk
steps.distractor: Stir the sugar with a third of its weight in water until it dissolves
steps.why: A dry caramel is sugar alone, so water belongs to the wet method. It melts from the edges and is swirled to colour evenly. The hot pan carries it on, so it comes off a shade early, and the cream is ready first because it boils up hard.

steps.title: Bake a New Orleans bread pudding
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a New Orleans bread pudding in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Whisk the eggs with the sugar
Whisk in the milk or cream, the vanilla and the spice
Pour the custard over the torn stale bread and raisins in a buttered dish
Press the bread down so it drinks the custard
Rest it 20 to 30 minutes, pressing once or twice, until saturated but not swimming
Set the dish in a tray of hot water and bake at about 175°C (347°F) until puffed and golden
Test near the centre: a knife comes out clean and only the very middle wobbles
Serve it warm, with the whiskey sauce poured over
steps.distractor: Use fresh, soft bread so it soaks up the custard faster
steps.why: Stale bread drinks the custard and keeps its shape, where fresh bread turns to paste. The rest lets the custard reach the centre of every piece, a water bath sets it gently without curdling, and the knife test says when it is done.

steps.title: Cook pralines to the soft ball
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a batch of New Orleans pralines in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Toast the pecans and lay out baking parchment before the syrup goes on
Bring the sugars, cream and butter to the boil in a heavy pan, stirring gently and scraping the base as it cooks
Cook to the soft ball, 112 to 116°C (234 to 241°F), or until a drop in cold water forms a soft ball
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the vanilla and pecans
Beat with a wooden spoon until the gloss dulls and the syrup thickens and clouds
Spoon it at once onto the parchment in rounds of about 5 to 7.5 cm (2 to 3 inches)
Leave them 15 to 30 minutes to firm
steps.distractor: Take the syrup on to the hard crack, 149°C (300°F), so it sets firm
steps.why: Pralines are cooked to the soft ball, not the hard crack, which makes brittle. Beating off the heat until the gloss dulls sets the creamy grain, and they are spooned at once, so everything is laid out before the syrup goes on.
